extracted.intended_audience: poets, satirists, literary readers, and critics (19th-century literary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Crafting a short satirical fable in verse (with prefatory remarks) that lampoons critics and other literary personages while aiming for concise force and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithfulness of character sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: All the characters sketched in this slight jeu d'esprit ... are meant to be faithful, for that is the grand point
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in satire or caricature, the sketches should be recognizably faithful to their models; honesty of portrayal is a primary aim and justifies a jester's sting. The author emphasizes that characters drawn 'in pure fun' are nonetheless intended as faithful condensations of traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable concision and pointed ending
rubrics_metrics.description: I began it, intending a Fable, a frail, slender thing, rhymeywinged, with a sting in its tail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fable should be light, compact, and deliver a pointed moral or satirical 'sting' at the close. The text foregrounds terseness and a purposeful final barb as central to the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sonnet unity and concentrated force
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all compositions, he thought that the sonnet best repaid all the toil you expended upon it; It should reach with one impulse the end of its course, And for one final blow collect all of its force;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing a sonnet (or similarly compressed lyric), aim for a single, driving impulse that carries to a decisive final couplet/line—the poem's force should be concentrated and cumulative rather than diffuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough proofreading and correction (errata hunting)
rubrics_metrics.description: As I ran through the leaves of my poor little book, to take a fond author's first tremulous look, it was quite an excitement to hunt the 'errata' ... In the edition now issued no pains are neglected, and my verses, as orators say, stand corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend carefully to errata and printing errors before publication; meticulous correction of blunders (including those introduced by the public/printers) is necessary to preserve an author's intended effect and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive digressions; preserve plot/coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: I'd apologize here for my many digressions. Were it not that I'm certain to trip into fresh ones ('Tis so hard to escape if you get in their mesh once); ... My plot, like an icicle's slender and slippery, Every moment more slender, and likely to slip awry
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive digression weakens narrative momentum and risks losing the reader; keep the central plot or argumentative through-line clear and avoid wandering so far that the structure slips 'awry'—or at least give readers permission/ways to skip the frippery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in facts, measures, and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure of your facts, of your measures and weights, Of your time,--he's as fond as an Arab of dates;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether writing criticism or allusive poetry, verify factual details, dates, measures, and references. Sloppiness in such material undermines authority and invites correction (or ridicule) from attentive critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain reader engagement; avoid tedium
rubrics_metrics.description: Any author a nap like Van Winkle's may take, If he only contrive to keep readers awake, but he'll very soon find himself laid on the shelf, If _they_ fall a-nodding when he nods himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to keep readers awake and engaged—avoid dullness or prolonged inertia in tone or pacing. Even formally ambitious pieces risk being shelved if they fail to sustain attention.
